How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The AI placebo effect, whereby the mere belief in artificial intelligence assistance alters user expectations and task performance, is an established phenomenon in human-computer interaction (HCI). Yet the cognitive mechanisms linking placebo beliefs to objective behavioural outcomes remain poorly understood. This study applies a hierarchical Bayesian computational framework to re-analyse data from Kosch et al. (2022, Experiment 2; N = 75), in which participants completed a word puzzle task under either a Control condition (no AI belief) or an AI Placebo condition (belief in sham AI assistance). We compared three models in which the AI placebo manipulation altered either (a) the mean of a prior performance expectation distribution (Shift model), (b) the precision (inverse variance) of that distribution (Precision model), or (c) both simultaneously (Combined model). Bayesian model comparison via Leave-One-Out cross-validation strongly favoured the Combined model (elpd_diff = 7.11 over the next-best model). Despite the winning model, group-level analyses revealed no statistically reliable average shift in either prior mean or precision due to the placebo manipulation (95% HDIs broadly overlapping zero), mirroring the null group-level performance effect reported by Kosch et al. Crucially, at the individual level, the estimated change in prior mean shift was strongly and positively correlated with observed performance improvement (r = 0.973, p < .0001), explaining the individual-level expectancy-performance relationship originally observed. Unexpectedly, reduced prior precision (not increased precision) was associated with greater performance gains under the placebo (r = 0.595, p < .0001). These findings provide the first demonstration that hierarchical Bayesian models originally developed to explain placebo analgesia can successfully account for individual differences in the AI placebo effect on objective task performance. The results indicate that the cognitive mechanism involves simultaneous modulation of both expectation level and expectation certainty, yet manifests highly heterogeneously across participants. We discuss implications for theories of expectancy-driven performance and for HCI evaluation methodology.

1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly embedded in everyday human-computer interaction (HCI), from productivity tools and recommendation engines to healthcare decision support and adaptive interfaces. Evaluating whether such systems genuinely improve user performance requires rigorous experimental methodology. A critical, and often overlooked, confound in this evaluation is the possibility that observed performance benefits arise not from the system itself, but from users' beliefs about what it can do. This phenomenon, the AI placebo effect, mirrors the well-documented medical placebo effect: just as inert treatments can produce real physiological and psychological benefits when patients believe in their efficacy, the mere belief that an AI is providing support can elevate user expectations and alter task outcomes. Kosch et al. (2022) provided the foundational empirical demonstration of this effect in HCI, showing that participants told a sham AI was adapting puzzle difficulty to their physiological signals performed descriptively better and held significantly higher performance expectations than those in a control condition, despite no actual AI assistance being provided.

While Kosch et al. (2022) established that the AI placebo effect exists and influences subjective expectations, the cognitive architecture linking belief to objective performance remains unspecified. In particular, it is unclear whether the placebo primarily shifts the mean of users' performance expectations, alters the precision (certainty) of those expectations, or involves both processes. Moreover, the marked discrepancy between a null group-level performance effect and significant individual-level expectancy-performance correlations suggests substantial heterogeneity that group-mean analyses cannot capture. Second, the cognitive mechanism linking belief to performance was not modelled: it remains unclear how this so called placebo effect manifests itself.

A productive route to addressing these questions lies in the Bayesian computational frameworks developed in the pain placebo literature. Anchisi and Zanon (2015), building on predictivecoding accounts of placebo analgesia (Büchel et al., 2014), formalised the idea that perceived or observed outcomes arise from the precision-weighted integration of prior expectations and incoming sensory (or performance) evidence. Under this account, a placebo can alter the posterior estimate of outcome either by shifting the mean of the prior distribution, by changing its precision, or by doing both. These models have successfully accounted for individual differences in placebo magnitude in clinical and experimental pain settings, precisely because they treat expectation level and expectation certainty as separable, quantifiable parameters. The present study therefore constitutes a direct test of whether the same computational architecture that accounts for expectancy-driven changes in pain perception can also explain expectancy-driven changes in task performance within an HCI context.

The present study applies this modelling approach to the AI placebo effect in HCI. We re-analyse the Kosch et al. (2022, Experiment 2) dataset within a hierarchical Bayesian framework in which objective task performance is formalised as the product of Bayesian inference: a prior expectation distribution is combined with a likelihood representing baseline ability. Under this formalisation, the AI placebo manipulation can affect performance by shifting the mean of the prior (raising the expected performance level), by altering its precision (changing the certainty of expectations), or through a combination of both. We compare three competing model specifications-Shift-only, Precision-only, and Combined-using Bayesian model selection, and then examine whether the winning model's latent parameters correlate with individual differences in observed performance change.

By importing and adapting computational models originally developed to explain placebo analgesia, this study moves beyond merely demonstrating that the AI placebo effect exists.

It tests whether the same cognitive architecture that accounts for expectancy-driven changes in pain perception can meaningfully explain and quantitatively characterise expectancy-driven changes in task performance within an HCI setting. The findings have implications both for theories of expectancy-driven performance and for the design of HCI evaluation studies, where uncontrolled expectancy effects may systematically distort conclusions about a technology's true utility.

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 The Placebo Effect in Medical and Psychological Contexts

The placebo effect refers to real, measurable changes in health, perception, or behaviour that arise from a patient's belief in an inert treatment rather than any pharmacologically active substance (Büchel et al., 2014). Mechanistically, placebo responses involve expectancy-driven modulation of neurobiological systems: positive expectations can activate endogenous opioid pathways, reduce pain-related neural activation, and improve outcomes across a wide range of conditions. Critically, the magnitude of the placebo response is shaped both by the strength of the prior expectation and by how certain the individual is about the expected outcome, a distinction that maps directly onto the Bayesian framework employed in the present study. Anchisi and Zanon (2015) formalised this within a Bayesian framework, proposing that perceived outcomes arise from the precision-weighted integration of prior expectations and incoming sensory evidence. Under this account, a strong, high-certainty prior expectation of improvement, the kind induced by a convincing placebo, shifts the posterior estimate of outcome in the direction of the prior, yielding real changes in subjectively and objectively measured performance.

This Bayesian framing provides a principled theoretical basis for applying a similar model to AI-mediated HCI contexts.

2.2 Expectancy Effects and the AI Placebo in HCI

User expectations are central to established technology acceptance frameworks. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM; Davis, 1989) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT; Venkatesh et al., 2003) both identify perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) as primary drivers of technology adoption and satisfaction. If AI placebo effects artificially inflate these perceptions by making a system seem more capable than it is, evaluations grounded in these frameworks will yield misleading conclusions about a technology's genuine utility.

The susceptibility of technology users to expectancy effects has been demonstrated across multiple paradigms. How an AI is described, whether as helpful, neutral, or even as a threat, substantially alters users' trust, perceived effectiveness, and subjective satisfaction, even when the underlying system behaviour is held constant. Users often develop strong mental models of AI capabilities that are shaped more by framing and prior beliefs than by actual system performance. Kosch et al. (2022) provided the most direct and rigorous demonstration of an AI placebo effect in HCI. In their Experiment 2, one hundred participants completed a word puzzle (anagram) task under two counterbalanced within-subjects conditions. In the Control condition, participants were explicitly told they would receive no AI assistance and that puzzle difficulty was random. In the AI Placebo condition, participants were led to believe that a sophisticated AI was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals such as heart rate and facial expressions, to adapt puzzle difficulty in real time and optimise their performance. Critically, no such AI analysis or adaptation occurred; the system behaved identically in both conditions.

Before each block, participants stated their numeric performance expectancy (the number of puzzles they expected to solve out of 40). Objective performance was recorded as the number of correctly solved anagrams.

The key findings of Kosch et al. (2022, Experiment 2) were threefold. First, the AI placebo manipulation significantly elevated participants' pre-interaction performance expectancy ratings relative to the control condition (H1 supported). Second, despite this clear increase in subjective expectations, there was no statistically significant difference in the average number of correctly solved anagrams between conditions at the group level (H2 not supported). Third, a significant positive correlation emerged between individual participants' pre-interaction expectancy ratings and their subsequent objective performance, a correlation that was notably stronger in the AI Placebo condition than in the Control condition. This pattern, a clear subjective effect without a reliable group-level objective effect, yet a meaningful individual-level relationship between expectancy and performance, suggests that the AI placebo operates heterogeneously across individuals. Understanding why some people's beliefs translate into performance gains while others' do not requires a model of the cognitive process linking expectation to performance, rather than a test of mean differences between groups.

2.3 Bayesian Models of Performance and Expectancy

Bayesian frameworks have been applied productively in cognitive science to model how prior beliefs combine with incoming evidence to produce perception, decision-making, and action. In the context of performance and pain, Anchisi and Zanon (2015) demonstrated that a Bayesian integration model, in which prior expectations combine with a performance likelihood in a precision-weighted fashion, could account for the relationship between expectancy and observed outcomes in placebo-controlled studies.

Applied to HCI performance, this framework formalises the intuition that a participant's final performance on a task reflects not just their underlying ability (captured by the likelihood), but also the influence of their expectations (the prior). The strength of this prior's influence depends on its precision: a high-certainty expectation (narrow prior distribution) will pull the posterior strongly toward the expected value, while a low-certainty expectation (wide prior) will allow the likelihood to dominate. This distinction between mean-level effects (where the prior is centred) and precision-level effects (how tightly the prior constrains the posterior) is the central theoretical question of the present study.

3 Research Gap and Research Questions

4.1 H1 -Model Selection

The Combined model, which allows the placebo manipulation to affect both the mean and the precision of the prior expectation distribution, will provide a superior account of the objective performance data relative to models that allow only a mean shift or only a precision change. Support for this hypothesis would indicate that the dual-parameter architecture developed for placebo analgesia transfers successfully to the AI placebo effect in HCI.

4.2 H2 -Group-Level Parameter Differences (conditional on H1 being supported)

The estimated prior mean shift parameter (p shift ) will be significantly greater (more positive) in the Placebo condition compared to the Control condition, reflecting inflated performance expectations induced by the belief in AI assistance.

4.3 H3 -Individual-Level Correlations (conditional on H1 being supported)

The individual difference in the estimated p shift parameter (Placebo -Control) will be positively correlated with the individual difference in objective task performance (Placebo -Control).

Participants whose effective prior mean is shifted more positively by the placebo are expected to show greater performance gains relative to their control performance.

5.2 Experimental Conditions and Key Variables

In the Control condition, participants were explicitly informed that no AI assistance would be provided and that puzzle difficulty was randomly assigned. In the AI Placebo condition, participants were told that an AI system was analysing their webcam feed, monitoring physiological signals (heart rate, facial expressions) in real time to adapt puzzle difficulty and optimise their performance. In reality, no such analysis or adaptation occurred; the system behaved identically to the Control condition.

Three variables were extracted from the dataset for the present analysis. The participant identifier (id) distinguished individual participants. The expectancy variable captured the participant's numeric self-report of expected correct answers (ranging from 0 to 40), recorded immediately before each task block. The outcome variable (numcorrectanswers) was the objective count of correctly solved anagrams in each block (also ranging from 0 to 40).

5.3 Preprocessing

The dataset was restricted to observations from the Control ('nothing') and AI Placebo ('camera') conditions. Data were restructured from long to wide format so that each participant contributed a single row containing their expectancy and performance scores for both conditions (yielding columns expect_Control, expect_Placebo, perf_Control, and perf_Placebo).

Participants with missing values on any of these four variables were excluded listwise. This yielded a final analytic sample of N = 75 participants. Two derived variables were then computed: a performance difference score (perf_diff = perf_Placebo -perf_Control) reflecting each participant's placebo-related performance change, and a baseline performance estimate (baseline_perf_data) computed as the mean of perf_Control and perf_Placebo across conditions.

5.4 Bayesian Modelling Framework

We adopt a Bayesian modelling approach in which objective task performance is treated as the product of Bayesian inference. Specifically, a participant's observed performance is conceptualised as a posterior distribution arising from the precision-weighted combination of a prior expectation distribution and a likelihood representing baseline task ability. This formalises the intuition that performance on any given trial is influenced both by what the participant expects (the prior) and by their underlying competence (the likelihood):

Both the prior and the likelihood are modelled as Gaussian distributions. The prior expectation distribution has mean µ prior and variance σ 2 prior , informed by the participant's stated expectancy rating. The likelihood has mean µ likelihood (set to the participant's average performance across both conditions) and a fixed variance σ 2 likelihood (set to the observed overall data variance). The posterior distribution over performance is then derived analytically from the combination of these two Gaussians, and observed performance is modelled as drawn from this posterior.

5.5 Model Specifications

Three hierarchical Bayesian models were specified, differing in which aspects of the prior expectation distribution were allowed to vary between the Control and Placebo conditions.

In all models, observed performance was treated as a draw from a Gaussian posterior formed by the precision-weighted combination of a prior expectation distribution and a fixed likelihood (baseline ability). The models differed solely in how the prior was parameterised across conditions: • Shift model.

Only the mean of the prior (µ prior ) was allowed to differ between the Control and Placebo conditions via a participant-level shift parameter p shift . Prior variance (σ 2 prior ) was held constant across conditions. This model tests the hypothesis that the AI placebo effect operates purely by raising (or lowering) the expected performance level.

• Precision model. Only the precision (inverse variance) of the prior was allowed to differ between conditions, implemented via a participant-level log-variance scale parameter log _var_scale. The prior mean was held constant across conditions. This model tests the hypothesis that the placebo effect operates purely by changing how certain participants are about their performance expectations.

• Combined model. Both the prior mean (via p shift ) and the prior precision (via log _var_scale) were allowed to vary freely between the Control and Placebo conditions at the participant level. This model tests the hypothesis that the AI placebo effect involves simultaneous modulation of both expectation level and expectation certainty.

All three models were implemented in PyMC using non-centred parameterisation to improve sampling efficiency. Group-level hyperpriors were weakly informative Normal distributions for means and HalfNormal distributions for standard deviations. The analysis code is available at https://osf.io/54ut2/overview.

5.6 Parameter Estimation

All three models were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling implemented via PyMC's No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS). For each model, four independent chains were run with 2,500 posterior samples each, following 2,500 tuning (warm-up) steps. The tar-get_accept parameter was set to 0.98 to encourage careful exploration of the posterior. A fixed random seed was used for reproducibility. Log-likelihood values for the observed performance variables were computed and stored for model comparison.

5.7 Convergence Diagnostics

5.8 Model Comparison

To address RQ1 and test H1, the three models were compared using Leave-One-Out crossvalidation (LOO), calculated via ArviZ's az.compare function. LOO estimates the expected log-predictive density (elpd_loo), which quantifies out-of-sample predictive accuracy while penalising model complexity. Pointwise log-likelihood values across both observed performance variables (perf_ctrl_obs and perf_plac_obs) were summed per participant and passed to the comparison function. Models were ranked by elpd_loo; the model with the highest (least negative) value was identified as the best-fitting model. Model weights were also examined.

5.9 Hypothesis Testing

All subsequent hypothesis testing was conducted using posterior samples from the best-fitting model identified through model comparison. For H2, group-level posterior distributions of the condition difference parameters (∆_group_mu_p_shift and ∆_group_mu_log_var_scale) were examined using posterior means, 95% Highest Density Intervals (HDIs), and the posterior probability that the difference exceeded zero. For H3, participant-level posterior means of the condition difference parameters were extracted and correlated with the observed perf_diff score using Pearson's r.

6 Results

6.1 MCMC Convergence

All three models converged satisfactorily. The Shift model showed no divergent transitions, a maximum R of 1.000, and minimum ESS values of 6,685 (bulk) and 5,593 (tail). The Precision model also showed no divergences, a maximum R of 1.000, and minimum ESS values of 3,848 (bulk) and 1,903 (tail). The Combined model produced one divergence across all chains and draws, a negligible number, with a maximum R of 1.000 and minimum ESS values of 3,189 (bulk) and 5,228 (tail). All models were therefore considered to have achieved reliable posterior estimates suitable for interpretation and comparison.

6.2 Model Comparison (H1)

Table 1 presents the LOO model comparison results. The Combined model, which allows both the prior mean and prior variance to vary between conditions, achieved the highest elpd_loo score (-473.03) and captured essentially all available model weight (≈ 1.0). The difference in elpd_loo between the Combined and the next-best model (Precision only) was 7.11 standard error units (SE_diff = 1.41), constituting strong evidence in favour of the Combined model.

The Shift-only model performed considerably worse than both alternatives.

6.3 Group-Level Parameter Differences (H2)

Table 2 presents the posterior distributions of the group-level mean differences between the Placebo and Control conditions for both parameters of the Combined model.

These null group-level findings parallel the null effect on average objective performance reported by Kosch et al. (2022), and are consistent with the interpretation that the AI placebo effect does not operate uniformly across individuals.

6.4 Individual-Level Correlations (H3)

Despite the null group-level results, strong individual-level relationships emerged between estimated parameter changes and observed performance changes. Table 3 summarises these results. Taken together, the results indicate that (a) the Combined Bayesian model best characterises the performance data; (b) at the group level, the placebo manipulation does not produce reliable average shifts in either prior mean or precision; but (c) at the individual level, the degree to which each participant's prior mean shifts positively is a powerful predictor of performance gain, and, unexpectedly, the degree to which prior precision decreases is also positively associated with performance improvement.

7 Discussion

This study provides the first formal test of whether hierarchical Bayesian models of expectancy originally developed in the pain placebo literature can account for the AI placebo effect on objective task performance. The results support a dual-mechanism account: the best-fitting model is one in which the placebo belief simultaneously modulates both the mean and the precision of participants' prior performance expectations. At the same time, these latent parameter changes show no reliable average shift at the group level, thereby explaining the null group-level performance effect reported by Kosch et al. (2022). Critically, at the individual level, the estimated change in prior mean is an exceptionally strong predictor of performance improvement (r = 0.973), while an unexpected reduction in prior precision is also positively associated with performance gains. Together, these findings demonstrate both the transferability of the Bayesian modelling framework across domains and the highly individual-specific nature of the AI placebo effect.

7.1 Both Expectation Level and Certainty Matter (H1)

The strong preference for the Combined model over both single-mechanism alternatives indicates that neither mean shifting nor precision change alone is sufficient to account for the data. This result has an important theoretical implication: the AI placebo effect in HCI cannot be reduced to a simple "raising of the bar" whereby users expect more and thus achieve more. Instead, the effect simultaneously alters how high the expectation is set and how certain users are about that expectation. This dual-mechanism picture is consistent with the broader Bayesian theory of placebo effects proposed by Anchisi and Zanon (2015), who emphasised that both the location and the precision of prior beliefs modulate the integration of expectation with incoming performance evidence.

From a TAM and UTAUT perspective, this finding suggests that AI placebo effects do not simply inflate perceived usefulness (which would correspond to a mean shift in expectation) but may also alter the confidence with which users hold their usefulness beliefs. If precision changes are not accounted for in standard usability evaluations, the pattern of results, including both inflated satisfaction scores and unexpected individual differences in response to the AI framing, will remain poorly explained. The successful transfer of this dual-parameter architecture from pain perception to HCI task performance suggests that precision-weighted integration of expectations may be a domain-general mechanism of expectancy-driven behavioural change.

7.2 Heterogeneity Explains the Group-Level Null Effect (H2)

The absence of statistically reliable group-level differences in either p shift or log_var_scale echoes the null group-level performance effect reported by Kosch et al. (2022) and provides a cognitivelevel account of why that null effect arises. The AI placebo belief does not uniformly recalibrate users' prior expectations upward; instead, some individuals show large positive shifts in their effective prior mean, others show small shifts, and still others may show negative shifts. When these heterogeneous individual responses are aggregated, they cancel out at the group level. This has direct practical implications for HCI evaluation methodology. Standard betweengroup or within-group mean comparisons are inadequate tools for detecting placebo effects that are highly individual-specific. Researchers evaluating AI systems should supplement meandifference analyses with individual difference approaches, including regression models predicting performance from expectancy, or computational models of the kind demonstrated here, to detect and characterise the full scope of expectancy-driven effects.

7.3 The Strong Expectancy-Performance Correlation (H3a)

The individual-level correlation between prior mean shift and performance change (r = 0.973) is remarkably strong and provides a computationally grounded explanation for the expectancyperformance correlation originally observed by Kosch et al. (2022). The Bayesian model attributes this correlation to the mechanism of Bayesian integration: participants who hold a higher-certainty, upward-shifted prior expectation will have their posterior performance estimate pulled more strongly in that direction, yielding better outcomes. In other words, the extent to which a person genuinely internalises the belief that the AI is helping them, captured here by the estimated shift in their effective prior mean, is the primary determinant of whether the placebo belief translates into performance. This has implications for understanding individual differences in placebo susceptibility more broadly. Factors such as dispositional trust in technology, prior experience with AI, suggestibility, and general optimism may all modulate the degree to which the AI placebo framing shifts individuals' prior beliefs. Future work incorporating these individual difference variables as predictors of the estimated p shift parameter would provide a richer picture of who benefits from, and who is unaffected by, AI placebo effects.

7.4 The Unexpected Precision Finding (H3b)

The most theoretically generative finding concerns the direction of the precision-performance relationship. Contrary to the prediction derived from standard Bayesian placebo models, reduced prior precision (i.e., greater uncertainty) under the AI placebo was associated with larger performance improvements. This is the opposite of what a standard Bayesian account would predict, in which tighter, higher-precision priors exert stronger influence on the posterior and hence on performance.

Several interpretations of this counterintuitive finding deserve consideration. One possibility is that, in the context of an anagram task where performance is highly variable and strategydependent, a looser, less certainty-bound expectation facilitates a more exploratory and flexible approach to problem solving. Rather than locking onto a particular expected outcome and pursuing it rigidly, participants with wider prior distributions may engage more openly with each puzzle, trying alternative strategies when initial approaches fail. This is consistent with research showing that reduced performance anxiety, itself often associated with lower expectation certainty, can improve performance on cognitively demanding tasks.

A second interpretation is methodological. The estimated log_var_scale parameters are latent variables inferred from behavioural data, and in a model that simultaneously estimates both mean shift and precision change, there may be identifiability pressures that couple the two parameters in ways that produce artefactual correlations. The positive association between reduced precision and performance improvement could partly reflect parameter trade-offs rather than a genuine psychological mechanism. This possibility underscores the importance of replicating the precision finding with direct measures of expectation certainty, for example, by asking participants to provide confidence intervals around their expectancy estimates rather than single-point values.

A third possibility is that the AI placebo manipulation, by framing the task as one in which performance is dynamically adapted to the participant's state, introduces genuine uncertainty about what performance level is appropriate, thereby widening the prior distribution. Participants who are most responsive to this uncertainty induction, whose prior width expands most, may also be those who engage most actively with the task, leading to better outcomes through increased effort rather than through the precision mechanism per se.

Distinguishing among these interpretations requires future experiments with direct measures of both expectation level and expectation certainty, ideally administered at multiple time points within the task. The current finding is nevertheless important in flagging that the relationship between expectation precision and performance under AI placebo conditions is non-trivial and not straightforwardly explained by existing theory. Regardless of which interpretation ultimately proves correct, the result indicates that the relationship between expectation certainty and performance under AI placebo conditions cannot be assumed to mirror the relationship observed in placebo analgesia. This divergence itself constitutes a theoretically informative boundary condition for Bayesian models of expectancy.

7.5 Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, the study is a re-analysis of existing data and therefore inherits the design constraints of the original experiment, including the specific task (anagram solving), sample characteristics, and experimental procedure. Generalisability to other task types, populations, or AI interface modalities cannot be assumed without further replication.

Second, the Bayesian model rests on specific structural assumptions, including Gaussian distributions for both the prior and the likelihood, and fixed values for BASE_VAR_PRIOR and VAR_LIKELIHOOD. Results are contingent on these assumptions, and sensitivity analyses with alternative parameterisations would strengthen confidence in the conclusions.

Third, although convergence diagnostics were satisfactory, LOO warnings about elevated Pareto k values for some observations indicate sensitivity to influential data points. The conclusions should be interpreted with appropriate caution pending replication.

Fourth, and perhaps most importantly, the model does not incorporate subjective outcome measures (perceived workload, satisfaction) or individual difference variables (personality traits, AI attitudes, cognitive ability). The hierarchical structure captures individual differences implicitly but does not explain them. Including such moderators in future models would considerably enrich the account.

Fifth, the correlational nature of the H3 analyses does not license causal conclusions. The association between estimated parameter changes and performance changes is consistent with a causal mechanism, but alternative explanations, including unmeasured confounds, cannot be ruled out on the basis of correlational data alone.

8 Conclusion

This study provides the first formal computational characterisation of the cognitive mechanisms underlying the AI placebo effect on objective task performance. Applying a hierarchical Bayesian framework to data from Kosch et al. (2022, Experiment 2), we found that the pattern of individual-level expectancy-performance relationships is best explained by a model in which the placebo manipulation simultaneously affects both the mean and the precision of users' prior performance expectations. At the group level, the manipulation produced no reliable average shift in either parameter, mirroring the null group-level performance effect, but at the individual level, the extent of each participant's prior mean shift was a remarkably strong predictor of their performance gain. An unexpected finding regarding precision, in which reduced certainty, not increased certainty, was associated with better performance, challenges simple prior-strengthening accounts of the placebo effect and opens a productive theoretical question for future investigation.

More broadly, the present findings illustrate the value of importing formal computational models from related literatures into HCI. By adapting Bayesian models of placebo analgesia, we were able both to explain a previously puzzling pattern of results and to generate a new theoretical question about the role of expectation uncertainty in performance contexts. As AI systems become more pervasive, understanding the psychology of AI-induced expectations-and the cognitive architectures that mediate them-will be essential for ensuring that evaluations of these systems reflect genuine capability rather than the beliefs they happen to inspire.

Kosch et al. (2022) established the existence of the AI placebo effect and identified a key puzzle: despite significant manipulation of subjective expectancy, the group-level effect on objective performance was non-significant, while individual-level expectancy-performance correlations were significant and condition-dependent. This dissociation points to substantial inter-individual variability in how the placebo belief translates into behaviour. However, the authors did not model the cognitive mechanism responsible for this individual-level relationship, nor did they investigate whether the placebo affected expectation certainty as well as expectation level. The present study directly addresses this gap by applying a hierarchical Bayesian computational model to the Kosch et al. (2022, Experiment 2) dataset. We ask three specific research questions: RQ1: Can a hierarchical Bayesian model that allows the AI placebo to modulate both the mean and the precision of prior performance expectations (the architecture previously successful in modelling placebo analgesia) outperform simpler single-mechanism alternatives in accounting for objective performance data? RQ2: Does the AI placebo manipulation produce statistically significant average changes in the latent cognitive parameters (prior mean shift and prior log-variance scale) at the group level? RQ3: Are individual differences in estimated parameter changes between the Placebo and Control conditions significantly correlated with individual differences in observed performance change, providing behavioural validation of the modelled mechanisms? 4 Hypotheses Based on the Bayesian theoretical framework and the findings from Kosch et al.
